newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lenin niece opposes re-burial of Communist leader.
newsitem.headline: Lenin niece opposes re-burial of Communist leader.

text.p: A niece of Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin, who says she is his only living relative, said on Wednesday she bitterly opposed the idea of removing his mummified body from the red marble mausoleum near the Kremlin wall.
Olga Ulyanova, a daughter of Lenin's younger brother Dmitry Ulyanov, warned that moving Lenin's body could have unpredictable consequences for Russia.

"As the only surviving relative of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin I do not give my consent to removing him from the mausoleum," the frail, silver-haired Ulyanova said, referring to a recent proposal by President Boris Yeltsin to consider such a step.
"His removal can lead to consequences which no-one can predict or even imagine."

Yeltsin suggested earlier this month that a referendum could be held to ask Russians if they want Lenin's body, resting in the mausoleum since 1924, to remain there or to be reburied in an ordinary grave according to Christian traditions.

"On June 19, 1941 Soviet archaeologists broke the taboo and opened the tomb of Tamerlane," Yuri Izyumov, chief editor of the communist newspaper Glasnost, told the news conference. "Two days later Nazi Germany attacked Russia."
He was referring to the 14th century Mongol conqueror who built a strong empire in Central Asia.

The idea of reburying Lenin, whose waxlike body is carefully preserved by a team of Russian scientists, started circulating in the late 1980s during the period of cautious liberal reforms launched by then Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
Russian liberals argued that Lenin, who created a totalitarian state and whose political heirs killed millions of people in mass purges, had no right to a memorial tomb.
Nationalists said Lenin, who was baptised into the Orthodox church, should be properly buried rather than lying in state like a pagan.
But the leaders of the Soviet Union or post-Soviet Russia have taken no practical steps to carry out the suggestion.
Opinion polls show that slightly more than half of the respondents disapproved of the idea of reburying Lenin and some 30 percent backed it.
The communists say Lenin, a sacred figure for them, should to be treated like some Russian saints whose mummified bodies are objects of worship.

"A famous Bulgarian fortune teller Vanga has told me that Lenin's teaching was as great as that of Christ," Izyumov said. "Vanga has said Lenin's ideas would be ostracised and later worshipped. I fully agree with her.
Professor Sergei Igolkin told the news conference there was nothing un-Christian about the way Lenin was buried.
"There is no strict ruling in any of Christian books that bodies should be buried in the ground," he said.
"Holy relics, including the unburied bodies of the saints, are being worshipped."
